utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Smith: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. How do you feel today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just provide you a reminder: If you are going to use the names of the people on the piece of paper in front of you, could you please use their numbers throughout your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, if you could answer the questions slowly. When we talk about individuals, think clearly about the individual and pronounce the name as correctly as you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we finished yesterday when you arrived at the KP Dom. You stated that a Risto Vucetic took you to the KP Dom and handed you over to a person by the name of Cancar. You stated that this person Cancar frisked you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cancar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that this person frisked you and then placed you into the compound.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know this person Cancar from before you arrived at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What job did he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he was an official in charge of the convicts who were serving time at the penitentiary, the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Cancar wearing when you arrived; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Cancar question you at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you with Cancar before you were placed into the compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He searched me; he asked me what my name and surname was. So it was a minute, a minute and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you why you were being placed into the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken after Cancar frisked you and asked you your brief details?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A solitary confinement cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big was this cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two metres by 2.5 metres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any beds in the cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in the cell when you first arrived at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many other people were in the cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 18 of us in the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew some; I didn't know others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the people you knew, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the solitary confinement cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those other men stay in that cell with you for that period of time, or did they leave before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 10 or 15 of them who were there from Curkusa. And Keletis [phoen] nicknamed Kele, came after dinner and took them to the room. I remained with a man from Gorazde who had been wounded. I don't know whether he was wounded or not. He was all covered with blood. He didn't talk about it; I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on your first night, how many people were in the solitary confinement cell? How many people slept there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and this man from Gorazde; two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who guarded the cell? Did anyone guard it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an official, Risto Ivanovic. That is where the official's room was, by the entrance into the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which building within the KP Dom was this? What was its name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right by building 16, that's where the solitary confinement cells were. When you enter the building, that's where this is, as well as the place where the guard is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think the witness means Room 16. There has been no dispute as to where the solitary confinement cells were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll move on from there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you sick whilst you were in the cell, the solitary confinement cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you sick of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was brought in. I don't know why I was brought in. At that moment, they let us go to have dinner. I could not have dinner because I started to vomit. I was sitting on the stairs by the kitchen. Risto Ivanovic walked up to me. I knew him from before. He was one of the officials there. He asked me what was going on with me and I said that I didn't know. He gave me a pill from his pocket. I could not even have any dinner or anything. I took that pill. I went back to the solitary confinement cell, actually he took me back to the solitary confinement cell. He locked me up as well as this man from Gorazde. I lay on that one bed. He lay down on the floor, on the tiles, and I don't know what happened after that. I just woke up in the morning. In the morning, I was a bit better, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during this time that you were in the solitary confinement cell, were you told whilst -- were you told why you were detained at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They only told us that we were supposed to give statements and that they would let us go then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the solitary confinement cell, you were taken to Room 16; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other people in Room 16 when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. About 50 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know these men or some of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some I did know, others I didn't. I knew 78 and 77.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of the men that you knew in this room, or of the people that you knew in this room, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Room 16?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there for about six months, until I first got out to cut up wood and to pile up firewood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said when you arrived in Room 16, there was about 50 men; did that number increase or decrease over the six-month period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 110, 120, it depended. Some slept in the hall, the room where we stayed, on tables that would be put together. Some had mattresses, others did not. We made mattresses from pillows, cushions that were left behind from the prisoners who had sat on these cushions before. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So everyone didn't have their own bed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, not everyone had their own bed, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe a typical day in Room 16? Were you allowed out of the room? For how long? Where did you go for meals? Just a typical day while you were in Room 16 for those six months.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Room 16, nobody could walk. They could only stay in this Room 16. When it was time for breakfast, lunch, or dinner, it lasted only five or ten minutes, the amount of time you needed to get out, go and take this meal, and come back. It took about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the times that you went for your meals, were you allowed out of Room 16?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when you went out for meals. You could only go out then or, if they came looking for you so that you'd come out to give a statement, then you could go to the administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What stopped you from being able to leave Room 16? Was it a guard or was the door locked or was it both or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The door was locked. Whoever walked out and then came back in, the door would automatically be locked. One of the officials had his office there from before and then whenever anyone went back in, he'd lock the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you keep clean? How did you bathe? Where did you wash? How often did you wash?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had toilets that were there from before, faucets where convicts used to wash and shave before that. We heated water in plastic bottles. We would leave them on the window sill so that the sun could warm it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there showers or baths in the rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often did you eat and what did you get for your meals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We ate three times a day. It depends, soup, sometimes there was a small can of liver paste for two or three men, and then a loaf of bread would be cut up into ten slices. What you got for breakfast, lunch, and dinner was not enough for a person to have a proper breakfast. However, fortunately, we still had some strength left in our bodies, and we were drained until the very last day of our stay. The more time went by, we had less strength and we had less concentration. You'd sit down, you'd get up, and if you'd get up very abruptly, you'd fall. If you were sitting calmly and then if you'd get up slowly, then you would not faint at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much did you weigh when you arrived at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 79 or 90 kilos, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your answer you said 79 or 90 kilos. Is that a mistake? Is it 79 or 80 kilos?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 79 to 80. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the lowest weight that you got to whilst you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness, please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I went to bathe, I didn't dare use soap to scrub myself because I thought my bones would fall apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, the interpreters have said they didn't get the weight that he had dropped to. If you could ask him to repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you repeat the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 48 to 50 kilograms, with my clothes on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you drop to your lowest weight? About how many months after you arrived at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at this weight? Was there a time when your weight increased?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it increased. Of course it increased. After six months, I started going out and working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did your weight increase as a result of the fact that you were working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The morning, at 7.00 in the morning, when you would go out to work, then you would have a snack around 10.00, and then you would have a double lunch, and you'd also have dinner. So that is how we managed to increase our weight when we worked. If you worked, you got it, and if you didn't, you didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this six-month period, what other rooms did you stay in whilst you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started working when I was staying in Room 16, but then I was transferred to Room 20 when I started working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay in any other rooms at KP Dom whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was also in 18, and in 14, and in 13. At that time, in 1994, I was in 14 and in 13. I went for my exchange from number 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you released from KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you charged with any offence whilst you were at KP Dom or were you convicted of any offence whilst you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your detention ever reviewed by prison authorities or by a court whilst you were at KP Dom? Was your case of detention ever reviewed legally, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only went to Zoran Vladicic to make a statement. That's all. And while I was at Zoran Vladicic's, he had a list in front of him, but I did not see that list. He asked me, because we were on good terms from before, we knew each other, and he asked me whether I had weapons and I said I did not. And then he said to me, "We can check that." From his drawer, he took out a piece of paper. I did not look at this paper, because he was on this side and I was on this other side. And he looked at it, and he looked at it and he said, "All right, you're not on the list. Nothing doing. Okay." So I didn't even look at, read what he had. I signed this little piece of paper and he said that I could go back to my room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time whilst you were at KP Dom, were you advised that you had a right to review legality of your detention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Serb detainees in the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those who were convicted before the war, they stayed there. They started coming in only in 1994, real convicts who had done something bad at the front line, who had stolen things from someone, who had hurt someone or whatever; then they were convicted and then they were brought in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the most number of Serb detainees at the KP Dom? About what period of time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many Serb detainees were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we left in 1994, on the 5th of October, there were about 100 of them detained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning, in April 1992, April/May 1992, were there any Serb detainees there then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any detainees, there were only some convicts who had been convicted before that and then they just stayed behind. There were four or five of them, whatever. They were also there at the prison farm, four or five of them. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked at the KP Dom, you stated earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier in your testimony that you worked, and when you worked you received extra food. When did you start to work at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood your answer correctly, you started to work after your first six months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you work for at the KP Dom? When did you last work before you were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time, the day I came back from the mine at 9.00 in the morning, that same day I worked in the mine, when I got onto the bus and went out to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd now like to talk to you about some of the guards at the KP Dom. When you moved to Room 16, who were the guards at the KP Dom? Were they people that you knew? Did they appear to be local, from Foca, or did they appear to be people from outside of Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were from Foca. All these officials were from Foca, and they worked as officials at the KP Dom in Foca before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that? Did they tell you or did you learn that from other prisoners or other guards that they worked before the war, or did you know them personally as being workers at the KP Dom prior to arriving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew everyone, the Serbs and Croats and Muslims, all of them who worked at the KP Dom, because I would pass by the KP Dom. I would stop by the restaurant for a cup of coffee; sometimes I'd come for dinner with my wife and children. Every one of them knew me too. Since I worked (redacted) for 17 years, everybody knew me and I knew everyone. But then, no one knew you; practically no one wanted to talk to you. Only Risto Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period whilst you were in Room 16, the first six months, did the guards appear to stay there day and night, or did the guards work on a shift basis? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In shifts. But there were guards all over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know about how many guards worked a particular shift, say the day shift, over that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the compound, about two, three, or four; and outside, I don't know. But within the compound, I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned some guards that worked outside the compound. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the compound, I don't know who was outside the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the guards wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they carried automatic rifles, guns, pistols; some also carried knives. Some played with their knives, throwing them at trees as if they were a dart board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they wear uniforms, these guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, some wore blue uniforms; some wore camouflage uniforms. It depended. At this later stage, they all wore the same kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who the guards' supervisor was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew. Mitar Rasevic. I knew him for 15 or 20 years. Before that, he lived in Samborska Street. He was the commander of the guards. I knew his wife, his mother, his children, everyone, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would he wear? What uniform would he wear, if one at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes civilian clothes; sometimes a uniform. We did not really look very carefully to see what people were wearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he work before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the guards at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would you see Mr. Rasevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, almost every day I would see him. Well, not every day. But he would come to our rooms; he would visit us. He told us not to try to escape because that would be fatal for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What led you to believe that he was the supervisor of the guards? Was it from what you were told or from what you saw, or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of us knowing for certain that he was the guards' commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that he was the guards' commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once Risto Ivanovic told us he was the guards' commander. I don't know. I think we were asking for some soap; we needed some soap to wash ourselves. He said, "I have to ask the guards' commander, and then we also have to ask the storage room keeper whether there is any there," and that is how we know that he was the guards' commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a person in charge of the whole prison at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mico Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a specific title that he was referred to as?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that he was in charge of the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we asked in writing to see the warden, but they never approved it, they never let us see the warden, and we wrote pieces of paper, little notes, and left them with the official. The officials collected those notes, and Savo Todovic would then come to explain to us what we were asking for, whether we were entitled to something or not, whether we could get something or not. Some people wanted to work; some people were asking for clothes. But from officials, we heard that Mr. Kunarac was the warden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your last answer, it reads that "But from officials we heard that Mr. Kunarac was the warden." Do you mean Mr. Krnojelac? It might have been a mispronunciation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Krnojelac prior to arriving at the KP Dom, before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but we did not communicate, because while (redacted) (redacted), as he went to work, to his school, then he had to pass by my shop, by the shop that I worked in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Krnojelac's job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Teacher. Teacher of maths.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see Mr. Krnojelac in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to Mr. Krnojelac and describe what he's wearing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has a white shirt and a jacket. He is smiling, and has got a finger on his lips.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For the record, I ask that the accused has been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you see Mr. Krnojelac at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was the first time that you saw him, about what period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. 1992. I think it was when he was going with the delegation to the furniture factory. That is when I saw him for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many were in this delegation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four or five persons in the delegation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you when you saw him walk towards the furniture factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Room 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what Mr. Krnojelac was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he wearing anything around his waist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a belt, and he had a small calibre pistol on his belt. Well, you couldn't really see, just the butt of the pistol a little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the pistol? Was it on the side, on his side, at the front, or at the back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you watch Mr. Krnojelac for and the delegation as they were walking towards the furniture factory on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't watching them -- for a minute, less than that. I got away from the window because you were not allowed to look through the window. You had to be at least a metre and a half from the window so that they don't notice you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you see Mr. Krnojelac the second time that you saw him at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, when Ekrem Zekovic was killed. He was standing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answer states that the second time you saw Mr. Krnojelac was when Ekrem Zekovic was killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ran away. Ran away. Not killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. That was the reason for my objection, and the witness said that he ran away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ran away. He ran away, wasn't killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be corrected then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wasn't attempting to lead the witness. The sentence started, "After that ... he was standing --" it wasn't clear whether it was Mr. Krnojelac or Mr. Zekovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see Mr. Krnojelac at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were lined up on the concrete path. He was standing -- there was Mitar Rasevic, Savo Todovic, they were standing one next to the other, and there was yet another one with them, but I wouldn't know who that fourth one was. I don't know him. I mean I know him but I can't give you the name, and I won't say it. No, it's not that I won't say it. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this inside the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were you lined up on the concrete path?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Savo was to lecture us that Ekrem Zekovic, that we did not kill him. That nothing was wrong with him. That we captured him. And then he took out room after room, 13, 14, and 15, three rooms were then. And then he said, "Celebici is wholly Serb turf, not a bird can leave it." And then he said, "I have 500 bullets. Had we not captured him, he would have killed you all. And he'd then kill himself," he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people were you with when you lined up, apart from Mr. Krnojelac, Mr. Rasevic, Mr. Todovic and this other gentleman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 15 of us, because room after room were going for exchange. We were not all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long after Mr. Zekovic attempted to escape from KP Dom was this meeting had? Was it the same day? Was it a day later? A week later? A month later? How long after were you lined up on the concrete path and lectured to by Mr. Todovic? How long after the attempted escape of Ekrem Zekovic was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there some trouble about the interpretation there? Try it again, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the attempted escape of Ekrem Zekovic, how much later were you lined up and spoken to by Mr. Todovic with Mr. Krnojelac and Mr. Rasevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not say that Krnojelac spoke. Mr. Smith asked him how long after you were lined up were you talked to by Mr. Krnojelac. The witness never mentioned Mr. Krnojelac saying anything. He only said that he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He certainly said that he was there. I don't think he said anything more, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's right, I misspoke, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You might try to ask that again. But first of all, let's ask the witness, can you hear the questioning at the moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A moment ago, I couldn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you should ask the question again, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after the attempted escape of Mr. Zekovic were you lined up and Mr. Todovic lectured you about escaping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days later. After three days, two or three days later, we came out after Zekovic escaped. He got as far as Bunovi, not further than Bunovi, and he did not go any further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Rasevic speak at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told us not to try that because it would be worse for us if somebody escaped or tried to escape, that he stood no chance because then there would be fire at our backs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitar Rasevic came to our rooms several times to tell us not to think of trying, or not to try to escape or escape or even organise the escape, and that was not the first time. It wasn't only when we were on this concrete path.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when Mr. Todovic spoke to you as you were lined up, how far away was Mr. Krnojelac from Mr. Todovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a metre, perhaps. They were lined up in front of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you lectured for? How long were you lined up on that concrete path?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of minutes. We didn't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Krnojelac was wearing on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had that pistol on his waist on that occasion or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. Yes, he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Todovic. Who was he? What position did he have at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he was the clerk responsible for the accommodation of prisoners, and that is what he went on doing. He assigned us to various tasks that had to be performed within the compound, outside the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whilst you were at KP Dom, what was his responsibility? Not before the war, but during your stay at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, he was the man responsible for the assignment of convicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which convicts are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who had been convicted before the war; Serbs, Muslims, and Croats who were incarcerated there. Because this was this prison before the war which existed there for all the persons of the former Yugoslavia who had perpetrated criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that in 1992 initially there were about four or five Serb convicts at the KP Dom when you arrived. In that period when you were in Room 16 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no. There were Serb convicts who stayed in the KP Dom but they did not sleep with us, in our rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, what was Mr. Todovic's role at the KP Dom? What was his function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assigning tasks. He was the one who assigned you to do this or that. Nobody could send you to do anything unless Savo Todovic did. Unless Savo Todovic ordered it, then you could not go and do anything. And it was his order, when you heard his voice and his order, then you knew that you had to do it. Nobody else could order it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "assigning tasks," are you referring to work tasks or other duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Work tasks. What you were to do in the compound, outside the compound, at the business unit, mine, the metal shop, wood chopping, wood collecting, Savo was the one who assigned you to all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Todovic wear? What clothing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depended on the time of the year. He never wore a camouflage uniform. I never saw him in civilian [sic]. He wore a kind of a sheepskin coat and that's why we called him Bunda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your last answer, you stated that he never wore a camouflage uniform, and then you said that you never "saw him in civilian." Can you clarify your answer? Would he wear camouflage clothing; would he wear civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say that I never saw him? Is that it, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not saying that you never saw him, I'm just asking you what he wore, generally. It's a bit unclear at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not really unclear. He has said he never saw him in civilian clothes; he never wore a camouflage uniform. I would have thought there's only one alternative left, and that was he wore some other sort of uniform. If you want to know what that is, why don't you ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that he didn't wear camouflage and he didn't wear civilian clothes. What did he wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the olive-grey/green colour of the Bunda, of the sheepskin, and trousers of the same colour. Not camouflage, but SMB, olive-green/grey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he mistreat people at the KP Dom whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was enough for us to see him pass through the compound, nobody needed to beat us or hit us because everybody was afraid of him. We'd all tremble when we would see him cross the compound, and he was there practically every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were people afraid of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't know. Don't know. I don't know why I was afraid of him. He always looked bad-tempered. Don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the guards, were there any other security measures in place at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. In the beginning, there were a couple of soldiers, but they were elderly men who stood guard above, that is, behind the rooms that we were in, next to the factory, I mean the furniture factory. That is where they walked up and down at night -- by day and at night, you could also see them. If we went to the lavatory, which was to the right-hand side, we could see them walk up and down. That was for a very short while, then they were withdrawn, and then active-duty police came who had worked for the KP Dom in Foca before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything on the administration building -- on the second floor of the administration building, in terms of a security measure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a machine-gun positioned on that administrative building. Because as you come from the window opposite Room 16, there was a machine-gun surrounded by sandbags and it was positioned in the window. There was always somebody next to it; at least, you could see the top of their head, you couldn't see their face. When we would get out, we would see the machine-gun which was in the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first see that machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three days after I left the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last time that you know the machine-gun was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which direction was the machine-gun pointed? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our rooms. Towards the exit from the building where we would line up in front of the staircase, before we come down to this concrete path, that is what it was firing at; as a matter of fact, not firing at but pointing at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll now ask the usher to place P88 on the ELMO, and I'd ask the witness to be able to point out the location where that machine-gun was placed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can use the pointer, Witness, and place the pointer on the building in which the machine-gun was placed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've shown it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this diagram of KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, the witness has --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. No, no, I was wrong, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For the record [counsel's voice obscured by translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That wasn't fully recorded. What you were saying was that he had originally pointed at building number 4, and then he said he was wrong.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wrong. I was wrong. I pointed at the school. I pointed at the school, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You tell us where you saw the machine-gun, would you, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He's now pointing at building 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained that the machine-gun was pointing towards the prisoners' rooms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The staircase here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the machine-gun in the window on the other side of the building number 2, on the compound side of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, because the other side is not shown. These buildings have been moved, as far as I can see, by a few metres down the Drina. These buildings should be higher upstream, upstream the Drina, not as it was drawn here. I can find my way around this, but other people will not, the way it's been drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can only say I feel absolutely justified, Mr. Smith. Why can't we use the plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'd ask that Exhibit P6/1 be produced to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be best if all of 6, so /1, /2, /3, /4, and /5, be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps P6/3, which is the second floor of the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Exhibit P6/3 in front of you is a plan of the prisoners' quarters and buildings number 1 and number 2 on that three-dimensional drawing you have just seen. Buildings number 1 and number 2 are at the bottom of the plan, and the prisoners' accommodation appears at the top, where you see Rooms 13, 14, 18, and 19. This is in relation to buildings number 1 and 2: You indicated on Exhibit P88 that the machine-gun was pointing out of a window in building number 2, the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you place the pointer on the room in which the machine-gun was pointing out of the window? Building number 2 is the long, thin rectangle --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite. It's the administrative building, the cinema, and where they had the school for the convicts who attended classes there before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Building number 1 is on the left, building number 2 is in the middle, and building number 3 just commences on the right-hand side of P6/3. Have you orientated yourself around this map? Is it useful for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be somewhere here. When you look up at the stairs of 18, 16, and 20, which you took down, then it was directly here. If this was the cinema where we were showing, so it is where the administrative building was and the administration, and it should be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For the record, the witness indicates the second room from the left, from the right-hand staircase of building number 2, on P6/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be better described in the room where the letters "DA" appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That is far simpler, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That is far simpler, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd now like to ask you some questions about the work that you undertook at KP Dom. You stated earlier that you commenced your work about six months after arriving at KP Dom. What was the first work that you did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My first job was piling up firewood which was in the compound which was used to cook food for us, and to heat rooms in the administrative building where the officials were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you do this work for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that for about three or four months, two to three months. And then Savo Todovic transferred me to Room 18. That was a room where people did not go to work. I stayed there until April 1993. Then he took all of us out, all of us from 13 and 14 who were not working. And as we stood there in the park, he was sitting on a bench, and he would just look at our faces and he'd say, "You go to the factory. You go to deal with the firewood." He sent some to the metal plant, others to the farm, and I heard that I was supposed to work at the factory. I worked at the factory all the way up to the month of October, 1993. When we were returning from the factory, actually when we returned from the factory, we went to breakfast. Savo Todovic was going towards the kitchen from the administration building. He stopped us. Actually, an official stopped us and he walked up to us and he said Dzevad Causevic and (redacted) should go to the mine. And he asked me whether I had anything to say and I said no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go back to when you first started your work, the wood chopping. How many others did you work with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five, four, six, it depends. Sometimes there were three. Sometimes people went to unload flour and then two would remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to an answer given at line 16, I would ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's already on the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other people that you worked with during the wood chopping, were they Muslim detainees, were they Serb convicts, or were they someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for about how many hours in the day did you do that work, that wood chopping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning at 7.00, when it is breakfast time, until 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who supervised the work? Did anyone supervise you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were always officials in the kitchen, around the kitchen. You couldn't just walk around. You could not leave the place where you were supposed to work. You could only go to the kitchen for breakfast, and then for the snack, mid-morning snack, and then everyone knew when lunch was. Then civilians who worked in the KP Dom, and the detainees, everyone went to have lunch, and then we went straight to the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the wood chopping work, did you have a break over the winter of 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 1992/1993, I paused during the winter and this pause was for about five or six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what month did you start in 1993 at the furniture factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The month of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what work did you do in that furniture factory in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I was putting bookshelves and that kind of furniture together. Before the war, civilians were the bosses there but then these bosses were arrested together with us, and they showed us how this was supposed to be assembled for a day or two. It is machines that actually did the assembling but then we just had to put in the right parts. Then I was with one of these bosses who worked there before the war. Then we started upholstering sofas, armchairs, and then sometimes when trucks were loaded to drive goods to Montenegro, to Niksic, then I went there to load these goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for about how long did you work in the furniture factory doing this type of work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few months. I don't know exactly how long we worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work -- during that few-month period, did you work daily or was it irregular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me about the factory?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you worked inside the furniture factory, you said that you worked there for a few months. Did you work there daily or was it more irregularly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. From Monday until Friday. Saturdays and Sundays you did not work. Sometimes, if necessary, you'd work on a Saturday, but that was seldom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what hours did you work at the furniture factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normal working hours, eight hours, just like the civilians who were our bosses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you worked inside the furniture factory doing the upholstery and putting shelves together, did you work on the roof of the factory, replacing the roof on that factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First, the lower part of the hangar, actually get the wood, and then it would be processed, and it was bullet-riddled there and then we had to cover it first so that the machines would not just stand in the rain as well as the wood that was piled up in those hangars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you started work in the furniture factory, inside it in April of 1993. Did you work on the roof of the furniture factory before that or after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the factory, I worked on the roof, the factory roof, and then I had this pause, and then I went back to the factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that you started work at the mine, I think, in late 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you work at the mine for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the mine, people would work intermittently. Sometimes you'd need to go there, sometimes you wouldn't need to go there. And then sometimes you would work at the farm and sometimes you wouldn't work at the farm. Sometimes there wasn't any electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what period did you work at the mine? From October 1993 until when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the way up to the 5th of October, 1994. There were only some breaks when we did agricultural farming work, when we worked in the field, when we chopped wood. I cannot say exactly for how long I went out plowing and when I went out to cut grass, and also when I went to chop wood, it was needed for heating the KP Dom because, later on, from the International Red Cross, we got these furnaces so we could have heating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what a typical day working at the mine was like; what time you started, what time you finished, where the mine was, and what type of work you did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would get up at 6.00 in the morning, you would get ready, wash your face, have your breakfast. The vehicle would be waiting for us at 7.00, sometimes earlier, sometimes later. It depended whether it would be a KP Dom vehicle, whether it would be a mine vehicle, whether it would be a military vehicle. Then we'd get there, say, around 7.30 and then we would have to change our clothes. And then you take food so that you could eat in the mine. That would be 8.00. And then you'd work until 3.00, or rather 2.00 or 2.30, you'd go out, take a bath, sometimes using cold water. Sometimes you'd have to wash in the stream because there would be no electricity for heating water. You'd bathe. Sometimes there would be a closed vehicle but then, most of the time, there was only an FAP truck, an open one, and then you'd just sit on that even if it were 15 or 20 below zero.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the work at the mine light work or heavy work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in my life did I do harder work, and never was I more afraid than when I worked in the mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you afraid whilst you were working at the mine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the mine did not work in regular shifts and then rocks would fall and it would be difficult to get from one place to another. You'd have to crawl on your stomach for about 20, 30 metres. The worst was when you had to carry a piece of wood so -- for four or five metres so that you would keep the roof up, as the miners would say, otherwise it would all fall down and crush you. We all had to do that, and we did everything by hand. We had to dig and load things by hand, and then it's easier when there's electricity because then it would be easier to do things not only manually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were digging coal at the mine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how much coal were you expected to dig individually a day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every one of us was expected to dig at least ten tonnes. Daily, about 100, 150 tonnes were taken out. If it were real coal, it would have been easier, but there was a lot of earth, soil in there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the mine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Miljevina, about 20, 25 kilometres away from Foca, towards Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many other detainees worked with you at that mine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends how many were needed; 10, 12, up to 17 at the most. It was never the same number. Someone would either get sick or someone would get injured at the mine. Nobody was a professional so they would get hurt easily, and there was always somebody who was away because he was sick. But only an official could approve this kind of sick leave, otherwise the only reason why one would be allowed not to go out and work would be sickness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who guarded you at the mine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they from the KP Dom or from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officials from the KP Dom. About two or three times we were guarded by the military police but we always had one official with us. There weren't enough officials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever work at the prison farm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'd fertilise the land, harvest corn, dig up potatoes, make haystacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the prison farm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About four -- three, four kilometres away from Foca, towards Godjevno, up the so-called Cehotina river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when you started at that farm? Was it 1992, 1993 or 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1993 -- 1993, I didn't; 1994, I was in the mine. And then when I worked in the mine, you'd work until Friday and then you would be off on Saturday and Sunday; but then on Saturdays we would have to go to work to the farm so that the land could be fertilised and that it could be prepared for plowing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For about how many days did you work at the farm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten days, fifteen days, approximately, if I were to add it all up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who supervised this work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll now ask you some questions in relation to the work generally that you had to do at KP Dom. Did you ask to do it; were you told to do it; were you ordered to do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I got out after six months, Vlatko took me out to work with the firewood. I worked there for a certain amount of time and then I was transferred to Room 18. And then, in fact, I stopped working and then I left from number 20. Once I wrote a piece of paper; I gave it to an official so that he'd give it to Savo so that Savo would see me and let me work. He called five or six of us in, and then we went into this little room, this little office of his one by one. Then this official asked me and said, "What do you want?" and I said, "I want to work," and he said, "Impossible." I was on my way out; I wanted to close the door. He looked at me and I looked at him, and he said, "You will have to go to solitary confinement," and I did not say a word. I knew where the solitary confinement cells were. I went to the solitary confinement cell. Obren Obrenovic locked me in there, and I was there on his orders for five or six days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said that it was impossible that you would work? Was that Savo Todovic or someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savo Todovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you why you were being placed in solitary confinement for making that request?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the reason; I don't know why he locked me up. Was the reason the fact that I asked? I don't know. I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you about the times that you did work mainly doing the wood chopping, working on the furniture factory roof, working in the furniture factory, and working at the mine and at the farm. Were you selected to do that work or did you ask to do that work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Selected. But when I asked, I didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you selected to do that work? How did you know that you had to work on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An official would come with a piece of paper and say such and such and such a person is going there and such and such and such a person is going here. On the paper, it would say whether it was the official who wrote this or whether Savo Todovic had written this, and we wouldn't know who had written it. But nobody could assign you to any kind of work if Savo Todovic did not assign you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were selected to do this work, were you given a choice? Did the person say, "Would you like to do this work" or "You are doing this work"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If somebody had a special craft, something he knew how to do, he would never do that, he would always be sent to do something different. If you refused something -- Muhamed Lisica had refused; probably he didn't want to do something for someone, perhaps he was nervous on that day or something. Savo Todovic assigned him to solitary confinement, working solitary confinement. He would be in solitary confinement during the night, and in the morning he would be taken to breakfast and then he'd work, and then he'd have lunch and then be sent back to the solitary confinement cell. So he could order you to work in a work unit and spend the night in solitary confinement, in isolation, without anyone else. If any one of us had refused work, the same thing would have happened to him as had happened to Muhamed Lisica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the work paid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any extra privileges given to you or given to detainees for working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, when we were cutting grass, we would have five or ten cigarettes, and of course, you'd get more bread than those who were in the compound or who were not working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serb prisoners work as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we cut grass and when we gathered hay, yes, they did go and work. But they were trying to get out just in order to get out of the compound. They would come to the place where hay was supposed to be loaded and then they'd run away. They'd go into the forest; they didn't want to work. Then they'd come back to the place where we would have lunch and then they would be there for lunch, and then after that, again they would go away. They didn't do a stitch of work; we actually had to do all the work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same guards that guarded the Muslim detainees whilst they worked, did they also guard the Serb prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't that you worked in two different places. I mean, you could not have one official guarding two different fields. So Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sometimes Serbs and Muslims had to work together; then also sometimes we would be divided up into two groups, and then there would have to be two guards. But if we were all together, then it would be the same guard for the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said that some Serb convicts worked in the furniture factory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the same guards in the furniture factory guard the Serb convicts as the Muslim detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody had to guard us there. It was inside, in a room. Everything around it was mined. There was an official who would be walking about the factory, guarding us and them. But we also had Serb civilians there, and we had Serb bosses there who were in charge of the actual manufacturing and they were responsible for us. So we didn't really need anyone to guard us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be a good time to pause here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. I should say that there is a special meeting of the President's Bureau at 1.00 today at which Judge Mumba and I are required to attend, so we will be adjourning a little before 1.00. We'll adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, earlier this morning you mentioned that you were interviewed by a Zoran Vladicic whilst you were in the KP Dom and he interviewed you about whether -- about whether or not you possessed any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times whilst you were in KP Dom were you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're not getting any translation here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The answer was "Three times."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You don't happen to remember what the answer to the previous question was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Merely the affirmative. Merely in the confirmation, he said, "Yes, yes."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Zoran Vladicic interviewed you, was that the first time, the second time or the third time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after you arrived at KP Dom did Zoran Vladicic interview you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 20 days or maybe a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the second time that you were interviewed, how long after that first interview was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After two or maybe three months, nobody ever wrote down dates or even thought about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was while you were in Room 16?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first interview, which building was that in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it on the ground floor, or the first, or second floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First. First floor. The same floor where that machine-gun was positioned. One or two windows behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second time that you were interviewed, who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Koprivica. Koprivica, but I don't know his first name. I've forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Koprivica from before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He worked for Maglic, and his wife was a lawyer and she worked for the hosiery factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what job did he do at the Maglic factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the second interview with Koprivica? Where was that held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second building at the entrance, at the exit -- at the entrance from the compound into the building to the right. Next to the reception room where you report when you come into the building, and that is to the left. And when you are coming in from the -- from inside the compound, then it is to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on the ground floor or the first floor, the second interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ground floor, because you -- when you start from there upstairs, then there are some stairs. I didn't even look. No, probably the first floor. As a matter of fact, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was this interview about with Koprivica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Koprivica interviewed me whether I -- because I had a firearm, a pistol which I had not reported to Vladicic, and that is why they summoned me for interview the second time. And then I was told that, in my apartment, they had found a contraption, a device which allegedly, according to them, I wanted to use to blow up a convoy of vehicles and heavy armament which was moving through Uzice to Gorazde, to Foca, down to Tjentiste and Trebinje. And they charged me with that and I never had anything like it, nor did I have it in my possession, and I merely denied it. I didn't have anything of that. And he said, "Right, if you didn't, you didn't." And I said I didn't. And then Zoran Vladicic came and there was another bloke, a dark-haired one but I don't know him, and we went to the gate from -- through which -- to the -- into the compound, and Koprivica said, "Off with him to the solitary confinement cell." And I looked at -- I glanced at Zoran Vladicic and he merely shrugged his shoulders and said nothing, and I was locked up in the solitary confinement cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how many days were you placed in solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two, three, four days. Don't know. I might have stayed -- I would have stayed there longer had not the Serbs who were there before the war who were convicts and they had -- they got drunk somewhere, and they had nowhere to lock them up, and Mitar Rasevic personally brought them and told me to get out and another one with whom I was there. They told us to get out and go to the room, and so Mitar Rasevic let me go to the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated earlier that you were questioned whether or not you had a pistol and whether or not you had some contraption that would be used to blow up something, whether it be a truck or a building. Did you have a pistol when you were arrested back on the 25th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use that pistol or did you have it -- THE COURT REPORTER: Excuse me. I'm sorry to interrupt, but there's just a problem with our -- my computer has frozen. Can I just have one second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: THE COURT REPORTER: It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are the translators able to tell us whether what has been typed is all that was said?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, the last question is missing and the answer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you any recollection of it or should it be asked again?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, we do not. It should be asked again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, you better ask that question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to rely on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you can't. You'll have to ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Koprivica whether or not you had a pistol or whether or not you had an explosive device in your apartment. When you were arrested --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- on the 25th of April, did you have an explosive device in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only had a pistol, which stayed behind in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were placed in solitary confinement, were you scared about what may happen to you whilst you were in solitary confinement or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't afraid because I knew that that was all I had, that pistol. I suggested to Koprivica to then go together to the flat and take it, but he said, "You don't have to go. We've already been there. Your keys are with Milenko Vladicic. Everything is all right in your flat. Nobody took away anything," and that was that, except that he said that they'd found that. But I stand by what I said, that there wasn't anything. Had there been anything, I don't think I would be alive today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third time that you were interviewed, how long after the second interview with Koprivica was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was all during five or six months from the beginning, and then for five or six months while I was in Room 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who interviewed you the third time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran, and then Zoran -- and then he said, "Well, pal, you should have told that," and I said, "Well, we've been told that after we gave the interview, that we'd be allowed to go." Because that pistol was merely a souvenir, a souvenir which was left to me, an heirloom from my grandfather, that is why I never thought of reporting it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was Zoran Vladicic who interviewed you the third time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zoran Vladicic tell you on this occasion or on the first occasion why you continued to be detained at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were most detainees at the KP Dom interviewed, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost everybody was interviewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where would those interviews be held? Which building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which floor these interviews would generally be held on; the ground floor or the first or the second floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who would generally conduct these interviews? You've explained that Koprivica and Zoran Vukicic [sic] conducted your interviews. Who conducted the other ones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from those two, there were two others, but I don't know them. After talking to others, I saw that others didn't know them. The third -- the fourth, as a matter of fact, I didn't even see him ask questions, I only heard it from others. The fourth one was with Koprivica when he was interviewing me, and they were in civilian -- those were, after all, all in civilian clothes. He didn't say anything to me, he just watched. He didn't say anything to me.
