utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zoran Vladicic and Koprivica, did they work at the KP Dom every day whilst you were there, say, whilst you were in Room 16?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, as investigators. He was an investigator before the war for the police, for the SUP. He worked for the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These investigators that conducted the interviews, do you know whether that was their sole job, to do the interviews at KP Dom, or did they have some other role as well as conducting interviews?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these interviews were conducted, were guards present? Firstly, I'd like you to answer in relation to your --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- interviews. Were guards present at your interviews?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the three occasions that you were interviewed, how did you get to the administration building? Who took you there, or did you go by yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official would call from the gate. I mean this official who is in the building. He has his telephone and talks to the gate, "Such and such is to come out." So you come out. And then there is the official waiting there and then Zoran awaits you. When I came out and went down to the administrative building, then he took me into an office, a small one, 2 by 3. There was a desk on one side and two chairs, or at least I didn't look much. He sat on one side and I sat on the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this official, did the official come to your room, your Room 16?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had to open the door to let me out because I couldn't get out otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say it was an official, was it a guard, a regular guard, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the official, the regular guard, and we called him official. That's what the former convicts used to address them, and they called them officials because they were their superiors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the guard take you to the interview room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness had just answered that he was taken over by Vladicic and took him to the upper floor from the guard. So once again, so the guard took you to the interview room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand the point of the objection. He has said --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness, when asked by the Prosecution, explained the procedure for going for an interview. That, in the passage, the inspector would take him over from the official and take him upstairs into the room. And then the next question was -- that is, I don't know whether to call it a question or an answer at the same time: "So this means that the guard took you to the room for interviews." And the witness has just explained the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He explained it in this way: He was asked this question, "When you say it was an official, was it a guard, a regular guard or someone else?" Answer: "Yes, the official, the regular guard. And we called him official." And then the question was, "And did the guard take you to the interview room?" What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, Your Honours -- let me just look at the transcript. The question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The question to which you are objecting, "And did the guard take you to the interview room?"

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. But the previous -- but previously, the witness had already answered the Prosecutor's question that Vladicic took him over from the guard in the passage and that he, himself, took him into the interview room. Page 42, line 24 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did you say page 42, line 24?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'll review the whole of that passage. "On the three occasions that you were interviewed, how did you get to the administration building? Who took you there, or did you go by yourself?" Answer: "The official would call from the gate. I mean this official who was in the building. He has his telephone and talks to the gate. Such and such is to come out. So you come out. And then there is the official waiting there. And then Zoran awaits you. When I came out and went to the administration building, then he took me into an office, a small one, two by three. There was a desk on one side and two chairs," et cetera. And then the question: "And this official, did the official come to your room, your Room 16?" Answer: "Yes." "And when you say it was an official, was it a guard, or a regular guard, or someone else?" Answer: "Yes," and I've read you that part already. Now, at best, it's equivocal, but you are asserting that his answer can only be understood as saying that Zoran, who is awaiting him, the guard having called him out, took him into the office. Is that what you're saying? Well, Mr. Smith, I must say I did not understand it that way when it was given, but looking at it in the transcript, I think it is perhaps equivocal. You'd better clear that up. Ask him specifically whether Zoran or the guard took him into the office. I'm not sure how this is important, but let's get it straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first time that you were interviewed, did a guard take you to Zoran Vladicic's office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The official did not take him to his office or to his room, whatever you call it. He only took me out of the room. He unlocked the room and told me to go towards the gate leading out of the compound. And I did, I went out into the lobby, and in the lobby there was Vladicic, Zoran Vladicic waiting for me, and he took me into the interview room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went across from Room 16 to the administration building by yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: By myself. By myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the interview was conducted -- the first interview, the second interview, and the third interview -- were there guards outside of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the interview room or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in my case. About others [as interpreted] --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How, generally, were detainees taken for interview? You talked about yourself, but what was the general practice? You said that most detainees at the KP Dom were interviewed. How would they be called for interviews, and how would they be taken there to the administration building, or would they walk across by themselves like you have stated?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 46, line 10, the end is missing, "Not in my case. About others --" and there are two dashes, and the witness said, "I don't know about others." So that this is also the answer to this next question of the Prosecution. We can ask the witness, but he said, "I don't know about others." And that says only "about others" and there are two dashes after that whereas he said, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to keep reminding you, but a point is not made any the better by repeating it time and time again. You've made the point. You say that where the dashes are, the witness said "I don't know." That's all you needed to say so, if I may say so, to make your point. Well, Mr. Smith, it wasn't heard. It certainly wasn't translated. You'd better get that cleared up, whether you go and ask him whether he is able to assist you about other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether other detainees were taken across to the administration building? Do you know how other detainees were taken across to the administration building for interviews, whether they were accompanied or unaccompanied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depended on the number of how many of them were going. If there were two or three, then they would be escorted. If not, if it was only one, then he would go on his own. If there were several of them, then the official had to take them so that they wouldn't do something, and somebody had to be with them in the administrative building while they waited their turn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that most of the detainees were interviewed. When detainees were interviewed at the administration building, did they generally go across to the building individually or in groups, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The rule was not to go individually. There were -- sometimes two or three would go, but I don't know if there were three or four or only one inside or whether two -- I don't know that. And whether somebody guarded them, if three or four would go, because two, or three, or four could not go in. It was all individual. You were only by yourself when you signed those statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were the Muslim detainees at the KP Dom, why were they interviewed, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were at the KP Dom, were you ever beaten? Were you ever assaulted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mara, Maric slapped me several times, I don't know what his first name is, I know him Maro, Mara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him from before the war or did you first meet him at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him before the war. I knew all the officials before the war because I worked at such a place that they came to my place to do their shopping. Not only officials, but everybody, all the peoples, all the Focians. It's not that we met; I go to work, they go to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Maric slapped you several times. Where did he do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the door into the room, the 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that inside the room or outside of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did he slap you? Do you have any reason why he did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything when he did it, either before or after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he took me out, he just said to me that if I were in his place, I -- if he were detained and if I were in his place, that I would stab a knife into his back and that I'd throw him into the Drina River. Then he hit me, and Vaso Pljevaljcic walked up and he told him to let me go. And then he did let me go. He opened the door for me and I walked into the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is Vaso Pljevaljcic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pljevaljcic. Pljevaljcic. He is an official. And this Vaso (redacted). An official, but a retired official.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know whether he worked at the KP Dom before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He earned his retirement pension at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you slapped? On what part of the body were you slapped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This side here. As I was standing there, he hit me this way, and with the back of my head I hit the corner, the corner of the concrete. I felt dizzy. Fortunately, Vaso came by. He'd probably gone on beating me had that not happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you want that recorded as to the demonstration he gave? As I understood it, he said he was hit on the left side of his face and that that pushed his head back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think that's all that's required to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this incident is referred to in Schedule A, number 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any injuries as a result of the slapping or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I felt dizzy, and I had headaches for two or three months after that. Then I had to go to Gojko to give me tablets that would tranquillise me. Gojko, who worked in the health centre of the KP Dom, allowed me to do so, and he gave me these tablets that would tranquillise me and that would make the pain go away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you complain to anybody about Mr. Maric's treatment of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who? There is no one to complain to. There are no complaints. There is no one to complain to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not complain to the other guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was pointless to complain. It was all the same. One was like all the rest, except for individuals, and these individuals were few and far between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any other detainees beaten at KP Dom, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they were. Everybody had to be kicked in the ass, begging your pardon. Or he'd kick you or slap you in the face just a bit, in passing, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. If we can just go back a few questions. I spoke to you about interviews and you said that most people were interviewed at the KP Dom. In the main, when were the interviews carried out? You were there for two and a half years. When was the most intensive period of interviews, if there was an intensive period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. 1992, that's when most of the interviews took place. They only took place in 1992; afterwards, there weren't any more interviews.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more specific than that? In terms of 1992, when did those interviews -- was it the whole of 1992 that the interviews were intense? Was it the last half or the first half? Can you clarify or provide more detail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this was from the 25th of April, 1992. The Muslims were arrested before that. That was the 18th. Then they were taken into the fields and then they were there for about five or six days. Then they were transferred around the 20th -- between the 20th and 25th of April. And then finally a real camp was set up where the prison had been, and then the Muslims started coming in in bigger or smaller groups. They would bring in 10, 20, 30 people. Every day the number went up. When the police, the active police, of the KP Dom took over, then the interviews started every day. Every day there was questioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they start every day? Was that April, May, June, July? What month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, immediately in April. When I came on the 25th of April, some people were already going in for interviews. On the 25th of April, when I was brought into the KP Dom, some were already going for interviews. Some came in immediately, as soon as they were brought to the KP Dom, whereas others went a month later or two months later. Perhaps they would spend a month or two there and then be taken for an interview. What the criterion was, I mean, I have no idea, because the criterion was not whether you came earlier or later. I don't know whether they did it according to the rooms where these people were put up or according to some kind of alphabetical order. Nobody knows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said these interviews, once they commenced, they commenced daily. Did they continue daily for the rest of 1992, or did they become less regular at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, every day. Perhaps they'd skip a day or two, like Saturday and Sunday. But all of that went on from April 1992 practically until the end of 1992, almost until the end of 1992. You cannot say exactly the day or the date or even the month when this stopped; nobody can tell you that. People were just thinking of how they could get more food, how they could get enough food to eat, or how they could get exchanged and get out of there. Nobody thought about anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were these interviews conducted; during the day, at night, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day. I went two or three times; I went around 10.00 or 11.00 or around lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned -- I can't recall, actually, your answer, but were other detainees beaten at the KP Dom, other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interviewed by Zoran Vladicic. I don't know whether it was the first or the second time. Well, that's not that important. The room next to me -- I mean, I heard someone being beaten in that room. I didn't know who they were beating, but I heard something. I heard someone say, "Now you can see how Zelja administers beatings." I was petrified. I finished my interview with Zoran. He called an official to escort me out because you had to be escorted out in front of this small office where the officer on duty was. I turned around and I looked and I saw Nurko Nisic walking behind me. Blood was flowing down his face here, on the left-hand side; he had a cut, a bruise. I don't know how I walked downstairs. My feet became smaller. I could hardly walk. I don't know how I got into the room. I couldn't fall asleep at all; I lay there. But I don't know what happened. I didn't dare turn around; I didn't dare look again. I was afraid to look; I was afraid that what happened to Nurko Nisic would happen to me too. So I don't know when he came back, whether he came back immediately ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After seeing Nurko Nisic with the blood flowing down his face, did you see him after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he explain to you what happened to him? Did he tell you what happened to him? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Whoever was taken downstairs and whoever was beaten was not asked because it was hard to ask people about suffering like that because that could happen to anyone. So nobody ever asked anyone about things like that; only if people would tell you about it on their own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this occur during the daytime or in the evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this incident is referred to at 5.27 in the indictment, and the individual is referred to in C-19 on the Schedule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you heard some noise coming from another room and you heard someone say, "Now you can see how Zelja administers beatings."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Zelja is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A worker from Valter Pejic, the company Valter Pejic. He was an electrician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this Zelja work at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the person that you've mentioned as Zelja at KP Dom on that same day that you saw Nurko Nisic with blood flowing down his face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only heard his voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you spoken to this Zelja before arriving at KP Dom? Do you know his voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He himself said his name, Zelja. "Zelja," he pronounced it himself. His last name is Zeljevic, and that's his nickname then, Zelja. He himself said what he said: "Now you're going to see how Zelja administers beatings."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise Zelja's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, that's going to produce a lot of problems in relation to redactions. I'm not quite sure whether it's going to make very much sense after it has been redacted. Might I suggest that you -- in fact, probably the whole of that answer will have to be redacted to avoid identifying the witness. You may like to ask a slightly more precise question as to how he recognised his voice, what was his previous association with him, and not worrying about who worked with him and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I would ask that that be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. But my concern is that you now get the evidence in in a form that will stay without being redacted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you recognise Zelja's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zelja himself pronounced his name, "Zeljevic," his last name, while he was beating Nurko Nisic. I didn't even know who he was beating there. But he pronounced his own name, his own surname. And then when I was getting out, Nurko got out too, and that's how I know that it was Nurko whom he was beating. And I abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I would just prefer to leave this topic. I mean, we can go into it, but I just don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think the only safe thing to do is to redact the whole of the answer, you see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we've asked that that answer be redacted in terms of protecting your identity, and that's the reason for it. You mentioned that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. Perhaps I did not understand very well which question, or rather, which answer from the transcript should be deleted. Could I please have the page and the line in the transcript because it would make things much easier for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment, I'm just getting it for you. It's page 54, and the question is at line 8, "And did you recognise Zelja's voice?" The whole of that answer, that is from lines 9 through to 17, has been redacted. It means that it will not be in the transcript which is published or in the video which is broadcast with the delay. The word "deleted" may be inaccurate. "Redacted" simply means it is not made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Nurko Nisic appeared to be beaten at the KP Dom. You mentioned that you were assaulted at the KP Dom. Do you know of any other detainees being beaten or assaulted at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. There's not a single person who was not beaten up. Some more, some less, others like -- I don't know. Like Rikalo Husko, for example, he was beaten up. He was taken away like many others, but I'm not going to mention their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you state Rikalo Husko, is he also known as Husein Rikalo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Husko Rikalo. His real name is Husein. His nickname is Husko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about his beating at the KP Dom? When was he beaten? Who beat him? How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Nobody knows who beat them up. Well, only they know, of course, who had beaten them, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how do you know that Husein Rikalo was beaten at the KP Dom? You said he was. How do you know that? Did you see it? Did you hear it from other prisoners? Did you hear it from other guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I did not hear about that from guards or anybody else. We just saw him when he was black and blue. Nobody had to tell you a thing if somebody would be black and blue or all in blood. There were some cases when we used a regular needle and thread to sew up peoples' wounds because there were some male nurses and doctors amongst us and they used an ordinary needle and thread to sew up peoples' wounds there were even such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this individual is mentioned in Schedule B-46, and also in Schedule C-21 [Realtime transcript read in error "41"].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see Husein Rikalo with his bruises, with his black and blue bruises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They passed by my room. 16, 18, 20, 12, from all these rooms, everybody could see everybody. Because all the windows faced the compound, the yard from all the buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is this man? What are his personal details? Did he live in Foca? What job did he have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know everything. He worked in Valter Pejic. He lived in Gornje Polje. He had an apartment of his own there. He had two children from two marriages, let me say that straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he still alive today, to your knowledge? Husein Rikalo, is he still alive today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can guarantee that he is not alive. Rikalo, a number -- well, let's not mention numbers anymore. But, yes, that's not important but perhaps it is important because it's important for the Court and for all of us. Let it be known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last time that you saw Husein Rikalo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: July, August. He disappeared in those two months, and the others, lots, lots and lots of them. Until the end of 1992, by the end of 1992, the prison had been halved. Half of the people had disappeared or were exchanged. Very few got in touch later from some European countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there might need to be a correction to the transcript. In the transcript, I have mentioned that this individual Husein Rikalo appears at Schedule C-41, it's actually Schedule C-21. It may have been my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It needn't be corrected. You have corrected it, and both of them are there and it's very clear what you are now referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that most people were beaten at the KP Dom. Generally, how did it occur and where did these beatings occur, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That occurred at the entrance, the entrance into the building where, before, packages, parcels were received for convicts. There were tables and benches there, and there was only 30 or 40 metres between there and the building where we were. And you could hear everything, everything resounding, like from moans and cries, and all that. Like from here where I am and to the other end of this room, of course you can hear everything in this room. And when we would hear these cries and moans, we would feel the pain, and every one of us would feel as if it were his own pain because we knew that our turn would come as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that these beatings occurred at the entrance. Which entrance are you referring to and which building are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exit from the compound on the iron gate, right on the left-hand side, below the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these beatings occur in the compound or did they occur in the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often, how often did you, yourself, hear these moans coming from this building? On about how many occasions did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A dozen times or so. You can't hear it always because sometimes you are in the lavatory or sometimes you fall asleep, and it happened in the evening hours, after dinner or before the dinner or during the dinner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do when you heard these beatings, when you heard these moans?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I do? Your hair stands on end. You cover your head up, your ears, so as not to hear, not to see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there doctors based at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a medical man there, Gojko, but he neither sewed up wounds nor did he give any medicines. Only 1993 or -- 1993, 1994, only then did we have enough medicines, and if you worked, then you could get anything you wanted, but in 1992, there were none. And what little there was, was taken out of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Muslim detainee doctors at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were they? Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Said Selimovic, a dentist. He was head of the dental surgery at the KP Dom. Ibro Carovic, Enver Cemo, they were all nurses, Emir Mandzo, and Cakim Causevic or something, I don't know his name but a Croat, Matovic, or Mate, whatever his last name was, a Croat. There were about ten or maybe a dozen physicians and nurses and such like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any people, any Muslim detainees that were interviewed or -- that were interviewed or taken to the administration building that didn't return to their rooms, they didn't return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, but names can't remember or dates when that happened. But, of course, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in 1998, did you supply a list of names of people that you knew were killed in the KP Dom to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you supply that list at your own instigation or on request by a staff member at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like to look at that list that you supplied the Tribunal to refresh your memory of other people that were killed, that you believed were killed at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can list them. I know them by heart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other people that you know that were killed at the KP Dom, can you state who they were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before that is done, if there is a list, do the translators have a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: They do have a copy, Your Honour. Your Honour, perhaps it might be quicker if I -- it's up to you, but if I go through the list, he's supplied a list of about nine names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bakrac, it's a matter for you, really. Strictly, he should give it, but if there's no real dispute about what is on the list, it might be quicker if we just have the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness said that he could list them by heart so I do not see why does the Prosecutor gloss Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. over that if he said that he could list them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In other words, you want him to give it by heart without reference to the document. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is what the witness, himself, said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm asking you what your attitude is. We're probably spending more time on this than it will take for him to do it by memory, but if you take the point, then you are entitled to take it and he will have to give the evidence from memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. It's -- let him do it which ever way he wants to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Smith, you may put the list in, as I understand that final answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After all of that, Your Honour, I might just start and then when he runs out, I'll put the list to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Husein Rikalo has not been seen again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you list the names of the people that you know were killed at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Munib Veiz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stopping there. How was he killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taken out of the -- taken from the dinner out of the compound. Taken during the dinner and out of the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this or did you hear it from other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw. Yes, we saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did this occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it June, July 27th/28th. I don't know the date. Can't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's C-58 on the list, Your Honour. Who else was killed at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halim Konjo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did he die?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also taken out from the line and taken to the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same time when Munib Veiz. It's all the same time, all the same date for all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Salem Bico.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: C-2, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also taken out to the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this line -- sorry, did you see this or did you hear this from other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt, Mr. Smith. I'm not sure that we're getting anywhere with this. So far, all the witness has said is that they were -- a number of them, all on the same day, were taken from dinner or from the line, whichever you prefer, and taken to the gate. Now, the next question I would think would be: Did you see anything happen to him? And if he says yes, you can get it; if not, you -- next question would be: Did you ever see them again? That's about the best you can get from this witness, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I mean, the witness has drawn a conclusion, and I can understand him drawing it, but I think that you have to establish that by inference in the end, not simply by this witness' own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll adopt that approach, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you saw Bico Salem taken out from the line, did you know where he was taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the exit gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he taken through the exit gate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody had to go through it to get out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him again after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of him being alive since that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Nobody ever ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Mr. Bico Salem was taken through the entrance, did you hear anything else? Did you hear anything coming from that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We heard from the bridge shots, and like when you throw sand into the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after he had gone through that exit did you hear shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back to Munib Veiz, did you see him go through the exit into that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything after he had passed through the exit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did, yes, because, later on, a man -- a few hours later, the man went there. They took one out; I can't mention his name -- or I can mention him. There is nothing disputable. But he went there with a hook if he floated near the bank. It is Mujo Dudic who worked for the administration, a cleaner. He cleaned the room of Mr. Savo Todovic and Mitar Rasevic's room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any beating after Munib Veiz had gone into that building or not? Is it just from what this cleaner told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, one could hear. They were taking them to the bridge, killing them on the bridge, and then throwing them into the water. And then we heard this one, when he came and when he pushed him away from the banks so that he would be taken away by the Drina. When I entered the room, a man said that he was found in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Munib Veiz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the man who mentioned he was found in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Munib Veiz was found there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else do you know was killed at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mesa Sofradzija. They all left then; they all left in one of those two or three days. They were all taken out of the line and through the gate, and not one of them ever returned or turned up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see -- Mesa Sofradzija, did you see him go into the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We saw them all. That evening they all disappeared; all those whom I listed and whom I will list, not one of them came back to the dormitories where they were before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of Mesa Sofradzija being alive today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else do you believe was killed at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mustafa Kuloglija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also when he went through the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of him being alive today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither heard, nor is he alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyone else that you believe to have been killed at the KP Dom, that you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murat Crneta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That same day when they went, all those who disappeared through the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of him being alive today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else do you believe to have been killed at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'd now ask that the witness be shown the list he drew up. It's identified as Prosecution 312.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at that list in front of you in relation to names of people killed at KP Dom, which you sent to the Tribunal in 1998, are there any other names on that list? In fact, the last three names, which haven't been mentioned, do they refresh your memory as to people who were killed -- you believe to have been killed at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not these two which I have before me. The two on top, no. Only Rasim Kajgana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rasim Kajgana, when was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was with them too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was taken into the building, did you hear anything after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about him, like all the others, like all the others whose turn it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uzejr Cankusic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When his house was attacked, he was wounded, he was wounded himself, and he was brought to the dorm. But what would he do there? They took him to the hospital and he never came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Salko Mandzo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one too, yes, Salko, he also left with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've finished that list now. Perhaps it would be time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay. We'll resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.48 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, you mentioned a Salko, I asked you a question about Salko Mandzo and you answered, "And this one too. Salko, he also left with them." Who were you referring to, he left with who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of those who were mentioned, they all went together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is Salko Mandzo? Give some brief detail about his background. What job did he have? Where did he live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lived in Donje Polje. He worked in Maglic in the furniture factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Salko Mandzo again after he went through that exit into the administration building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a number of individuals that went through the exit into that administration building. Did you hear any beatings after those people had gone into the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not hear any beatings. We just heard a vehicle ignited and it left in front of the Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear where that vehicle went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Went towards the bridge. Towards town, up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear anything after that, after it went towards the bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that most of the detainees at the KP Dom were beaten, and you also mentioned on about a dozen occasions you could hear moans and the sounds of beatings coming from the administration building. How did this knowledge of the beatings and hearing the beatings, how did that affect you whilst you were at KP Dom during the time that it was occurring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is too terrible to be described. At some moments, you'd feel your blood freeze because you'd think that what was happening to these others who were being taken out of the KP Dom and never returning could actually happen to you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross ever visit you at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many times did they visit you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think we were registered in 1992, 1993 -- 1993. Sometime in August, I think they came for the first time. That's like a year and a half. When I got this paper from the International Red Cross, we had been registered for some three or four months in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were released from KP Dom in October 1994, did you receive a certificate from the Red Cross indicating the dates that you were detained at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the International Red Cross, I got that, and I also got it from this international commission, this commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina. From Hamed Masovic [phoen], I got this paper when they registered us. Under this same number, we have this little card, and on this card, there is like this little number which is like a code, and that has to do with the International Red Cross also. Whether I was detained under such and such a number, you see, so that number is on that little card.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask the witness be shown Prosecution identification number 315 and 313 and the two translations, please. If 315 could be shown first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, looking at the document marked 315 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It should not go on the ELMO because it's got his name on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the document number 315, the Red Cross certificate, is that the certificate that was given to you on your release?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I got afterwards. After 10 or 15 days, from the International Red Cross from Zagreb, this is this paper with this seal and this is what I got from this commission of ours in Sarajevo when I was exchanged. Yes, that's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the certificate that you are referring to, the one that you got from the commission in Sarajevo is marked 313 at the top right-hand corner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask to tender those two certificates and the translation which is 313A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be exhibits P315, 313 and 313A. All of them will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were in custody at the KP Dom from the 25th of April, 1992, and you were released on the 6th of October, 1994. For that two and a half years of detention at the KP Dom, how has that affected you psychologically? How has that affected you, how you view life, how you feel and how you live today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How I feel? First of all, I've lost my health. Secondly, I've lost 30 or 40 per cent of my memory. Thirdly, what can I say? I lost everything I had: My house, my property, my apartment, the apartment I had. What could I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all I wish to apologise to you and to give an explanation because sometimes, or quite often, I repeat what I have said. And I forget that the interpretation comes in a bit later. I look at the Trial Chamber and I have the feeling that what I said has not come across, but I'll try to prevent it from happening again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can assure you, Mr. Bakrac, we listen to everything you say with interest. We just don't like hearing it several times. So just wait and pause after you've said it the first time, let us hear the interpretation, and then we'll get on with it. But thank you for the apology. Cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to introduce myself to the witness. Good afternoon, I am Mihajlo Bakrac, attorney at law. I am one of the Defence counsel for the accused Milorad Krnojelac. Before the break, you talked about when you saw the accused, you said you first saw him with a delegation as he was going to the furniture factory. Can you tell us when this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992. I cannot give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give me the approximate month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you say the last time you saw the warden was that Ekrem Zekovic ran away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you approximately remember the year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember. We did not think about that then. We did not think about the dates then. We just wondered what would happen to us. That's the only thing we thought about. I can probably say that it was in 1994, 1993, perhaps. The end of 1993, beginning of 1994. I don't want to say anything specific because I cannot tell you things I'm not sure about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it strange to you that at the moment when the incident with Ekrem Zekovic occurred, the warden of the KP Dom was just standing there and Savo Todovic was addressing you, Savo Todovic was making a speech to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savo Todovic spoke to us all the time. I don't know what the reason was, whether Mr. Mico Krnojelac let Savo take care of us or whether it was Mr. Krnojelac who was taking care of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 29th of October, 1998, did you make a statement to the investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you bring your chair up a little bit closer to the microphones because the interpreters are having difficulty hearing you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember having said in that statement that Savo Todovic was the most powerful man at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most powerful? For us he was the most powerful. He gave us orders as to what we were supposed to do. But who gave him orders, we thought it was the warden of the KP Dom who gave him orders for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read your sentence: "Although he was not warden of the prison, he was the most powerful person there."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, the most powerful. Most probably Mico Krnojelac would leave the orders and carrying them out to him. Perhaps Mr. Mico Krnojelac didn't want to be involved in such matters. I saw him only once or twice after that. I went to cut grass at Dobricava, Niko, Coprata Slatine [phoen]. Savo would come to see us; Mr. Mico never did. I would also fertilise the land, harvest corn at the farm. We did all sorts of things. But I personally never saw Mr. Mico Krnojelac at the farm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you stated that Savo Todovic, when he made this speech to you, said that he would cut your meals by a third and forbid you to go out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Only the farm worked and the metal shop worked, and as the days went by, he started letting people -- some people, not everybody the way he did before, but he let some people work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that on the 21st of October, 1994 you gave a statement at the Security Service Centre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that statement, when you mentioned the Zekovic incident, you did not mention at all that Krnojelac was present when Savo Todovic was making his speech.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly I didn't then. At that time, it was important to get out, and when you got out, you didn't even know where you were, whether you were in heaven or on earth. It was just important to recuperate and to come to, sort of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that from October 1993 you went to work in the mine in Miljevina. Can you agree with me if I say that you were among the first persons who went to work in the mine in Miljevina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-198 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first persons who went to work in the mine, that was in 1992, those were the engineering and mining people. I don't know. They were all returned from there because they were afraid that these guys would escape. Then all of that was stopped altogether and then it continued.
